scenes.tts: How can actin move backward while a crawling cell's edge moves forward? How can microtubules slide lengthwise while a cilium bends? Both puzzles start with internal motion whose visible output points elsewhere.
scenes.visual: Open immediately on one full-frame schematic workbench split by a thin vertical line. Left: a broad grey cell membrane above a substrate, with a teal actin mesh drifting left while its green leading edge creeps right. Right: two long doublets slide lengthwise while their shared bundle curves upward. White question marks connect each internal arrow to its visible output. Keep both machines moving, with a small 'schematic' label visible.
scenes.narration: How can actin move backward while a crawling cell's edge moves forward? How can microtubules slide lengthwise while a cilium bends? Both puzzles start with internal motion whose visible output points elsewhere.

scenes.tts: Keep both machines on one bench. In each, polymers and motors create internal motion. Our first picture holds those motion generators steady and changes one constraint. Then we will ask what it leaves out.
scenes.visual: Carry the same split bench. Briefly place the title across the centre, then shrink it to the top. Label the left half 'crawling edge' and the right half 'motile axoneme'. Internal arrows pulse; green output arrows remain question marks. Mark the whole picture 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: Keep both machines on one bench. In each, polymers and motors create internal motion. Our first picture holds those motion generators steady and changes one constraint. Then we will ask what it leaves out.

scenes.tts: Start at a lamellipodium, the thin actin-rich front of a crawling cell. Actin subunits extend filaments relative to the network behind. The substrate is the surface beneath the cell; the edge moves forward relative to it.
scenes.visual: Zoom into the left half without changing its layout. Teal actin filaments fill most of the frame height. Yellow blocks join their tips one by one, lifting the grey membrane rightward. A fixed ruler labelled 'substrate' makes the green edge displacement visible. Keep the right axoneme dimly visible at the frame edge.
scenes.narration: Start at a lamellipodium, the thin actin-rich front of a crawling cell. Actin subunits extend filaments relative to the network behind. The substrate is the surface beneath the cell; the edge moves forward relative to it.

scenes.tts: Small fluorescent markers called speckles reveal the actin network moving backward over the substrate. That motion is retrograde flow. At a lamellipodial edge, polymerization adds forward speed, while retrograde flow subtracts it. Growth is measured against the network; edge and flow against the substrate.
scenes.visual: Keep the left machine. Bright teal speckles drift left across the fixed substrate ruler while yellow blocks continue joining at the right edge. Transform the arrows into a schematic velocity bar: forward polymerization minus rearward flow equals the shorter green edge-speed bar. Label the two reference frames, and show no invented values.
scenes.narration: Small fluorescent markers called speckles reveal the actin network moving backward over the substrate. That motion is retrograde flow. At a lamellipodial edge, polymerization adds forward speed, while retrograde flow subtracts it. Growth is measured against the network; edge and flow against the substrate.

scenes.tts: An integrin is a membrane receptor that grips extracellular matrix and connects through linker proteins to actin. Together they act like a clutch: polymerization is the engine, and adhesion transmits its motion. Integrin coupling can reduce backward slip in this simple crawling model, so more growth appears as edge advance.
scenes.visual: Orange integrin receptors rise from the membrane, grip the substrate outside and connect through short linker proteins to the teal mesh inside. Show the labels 'integrin', 'linker' and 'clutch'. As coupling engages, speckle motion slows while yellow addition continues unchanged; the green edge arrow lengthens. Do not show the rear or imply whole-cell speed.
scenes.narration: An integrin is a membrane receptor that grips extracellular matrix and connects through linker proteins to actin. Together they act like a clutch: polymerization is the engine, and adhesion transmits its motion. Integrin coupling can reduce backward slip in this simple crawling model, so more growth appears as edge advance.

scenes.tts: Now move to a motile cilium, a hairlike projection that beats. Its axoneme is the internal microtubule core. In the classic nine-plus-two layout, nine doublets surround two central microtubules. Each doublet contains a complete ay tubule fused to an incomplete bee tubule.
scenes.caption: Now move to a motile cilium, a hairlike projection that beats. Its axoneme is the internal microtubule core. In the classic 9+2 layout, nine doublets surround two central microtubules. Each doublet contains a complete A-tubule fused to an incomplete B-tubule.
scenes.visual: Pan smoothly to the right half. First show the cilium outline, then build its 9+2 cross-section. Zoom to two neighbouring doublets. Draw each doublet as its own blue A-tubule fused to a purple B-tubule; never colour one whole doublet as A and the other as B. Keep a small 'schematic' label.
scenes.narration: Now move to a motile cilium, a hairlike projection that beats. Its axoneme is the internal microtubule core. In the classic 9+2 layout, nine doublets surround two central microtubules. Each doublet contains a complete A-tubule fused to an incomplete B-tubule.

scenes.tts: In motile axonemes, dynein motors slide neighbouring doublets. Their arms anchor on one doublet's ay tubule and grip the neighbour's bee tubule. A head steps toward that neighbour's base. Seen from the other side, the same action pushes the neighbour toward its tip.
scenes.caption: In motile axonemes, dynein motors slide neighbouring doublets. Their arms anchor on one doublet's A-tubule and grip the neighbour's B-tubule. A head steps toward that neighbour's base. Seen from the other side, the same action pushes the neighbour toward its tip.
scenes.visual: Carry the two correctly fused doublets. Yellow dynein arms are anchored only on the blue A-tubule of one doublet and repeatedly grip the adjacent purple B-tubule. Animate a white motor-head arrow toward the neighbour's base and a matching relative-motion arrow toward its tip. Label both viewpoints briefly.
scenes.narration: In motile axonemes, dynein motors slide neighbouring doublets. Their arms anchor on one doublet's A-tubule and grip the neighbour's B-tubule. A head steps toward that neighbour's base. Seen from the other side, the same action pushes the neighbour toward its tip.

scenes.tts: In the simplest picture, focus on two neighbouring doublets. Free doublets would pass one another. Relative sliding creates shear, a lengthwise offset. In motile axonemes, links that resist sliding, with base anchoring, turn sliding into bending. Here the motors stay unchanged.
scenes.visual: Add a large orange basal anchor and several orange interdoublet links. Define 'shear' on screen as 'lengthwise offset'. Dynein continues stepping, but the linked pair progressively curves instead of sliding apart. Label the links 'resist sliding', not 'resist separation'. Keep the drawing marked 'simple schematic'.
scenes.narration: In the simplest picture, focus on two neighbouring doublets. Free doublets would pass one another. Relative sliding creates shear, a lengthwise offset. In motile axonemes, links that resist sliding, with base anchoring, turn sliding into bending. Here the motors stay unchanged.

scenes.tts: A real bend needs more: dyneins on opposite sides must not be equally active. Motor control selects which side is more active. The constraint shapes the output, while regulation helps choose where the bend forms.
scenes.visual: Pull back to the full 9+2 ring. Brighten dyneins on one side and dim those opposite; curve the bundle toward one side. Add a small control dial labelled 'which motors are active'. Keep the orange links and base visible so regulation and resistance appear together.
scenes.narration: A real bend needs more: dyneins on opposite sides must not be equally active. Motor control selects which side is more active. The constraint shapes the output, while regulation helps choose where the bend forms.

scenes.tts: Predict both outcomes while the motion generators stay unchanged. Release the crawling clutch, and cut the axonemal links. What happens to edge advance and to the doublets?
scenes.visual: Return to the split bench. On the left, orange clutch blocks show open-lock symbols. On the right, red cut marks appear over each orange link. Keep the question in large white text across the top; pause both machines at the instant before release.
scenes.narration: Predict both outcomes while the motion generators stay unchanged. Release the crawling clutch, and cut the axonemal links. What happens to edge advance and to the doublets?

scenes.visual: Hold the prediction question and both poised machines. Let only tiny teal speckles and small yellow dynein heads shimmer, without revealing either outcome.

scenes.tts: With the clutch released, more actin motion becomes retrograde flow, so the edge advances less in this simple case. With links cut, dynein makes doublets slide apart instead of bending. The motors still work; the changed constraint reveals a different output.
scenes.visual: Reveal both answers together. Left: clutch blocks drop away, speckles accelerate left and the green edge arrow shrinks. Right: cut links fade, the correctly drawn doublets slide lengthwise past one another and the bend arrow disappears. Keep the base visible and mark both results 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: With the clutch released, more actin motion becomes retrograde flow, so the edge advances less in this simple case. With links cut, dynein makes doublets slide apart instead of bending. The motors still work; the changed constraint reveals a different output.

scenes.tts: The two machines share a logic, not every detail. Polymers and motors create internal relative motion. With motors unchanged, a mechanical constraint helps decide whether motion slips, advances, slides apart, or bends. In these two systems, constraints and motor control shape the visible output of internal motion.
scenes.visual: Transform the split bench into one comparison. Internal-motion arrows pass through an orange constraint gate beside a magenta motor-control dial, then emerge as green output arrows. Restore the crawling edge and bent axoneme behind them. End with both systems moving slowly.
scenes.narration: The two machines share a logic, not every detail. Polymers and motors create internal relative motion. With motors unchanged, a mechanical constraint helps decide whether motion slips, advances, slides apart, or bends. In these two systems, constraints and motor control shape the visible output of internal motion.

scenes.visual: End card over the dim carried workbench: 'Constraints and motor control shape internal motion into visible movement.' Keep the ten-word line large and centred, with slow speckle drift and a gently flexing axoneme.
